summary: This 1983 memo is a survey of how far various hosts had implemented parts of SMTP, the Internet mail protocol. It specifies nothing itself and is only a snapshot of implementation status at the time, which was expected to change.

plainLanguage.summary: A teacher walks round the class and writes down who has finished which part of the homework. The list is only true for that day.

questions: what was smtp implementation status in 1983
how many internet hosts supported smtp in 1983
what bugs did the smtp survey find
subtitle: A 1983 snapshot of how the Internet's mail servers handled the new protocol.

tldr.problem: The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol was newly standardized, but implementers were deploying it with significant variations and bugs. Observers needed to understand what hosts actually supported and how they behaved.
tldr.mechanism: A survey tested 483 Internet hosts between May and August 1983 to see which accepted connections from different networks, which recognized the postmaster user, and which rejected mail to nonexistent users. Notable bugs were documented, including incorrect reply codes and improper handling of VRFY and RSET commands.
tldr.outcome: The survey revealed that 17% of hosts claiming SMTP support could not accept connections, and about 40% of connectable hosts had at least one of three significant implementation problems. The findings helped identify where protocol implementations diverged from RFC 821.

today: RFC 876 documents a survey of SMTP implementations as they existed in mid-1983. Although the memo is historic, it is a valuable snapshot of early Internet mail system variability and the kinds of interoperability problems that prompted RFC 821 to be created and revised.

sections.title: A Snapshot of SMTP Compliance
sections.content:
RFC 876 is a memo reporting on a survey of SMTP servers run from May to August 1983. David Smallberg at ISI tested 483 Internet hosts to see how many actually implemented the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, which had been standardized the year before in RFC 821. The survey was not meant to be an official standard or formal specification, but rather a real-world check on implementation status at a moment when the Internet was still small enough to survey manually.

The hosts were tested from two ISI machines running 4.1BSD Unix: ISI-VAXA on the Arpanet (a Class A network) and ISI-MOE on ISI-Net (a Class B network). The tests checked whether each host would accept a connection, whether it recognized the user postmaster, and whether it correctly rejected mail sent to a fake user.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone at a research center picked 483 computers on the Internet and tried to send them mail to see which ones worked and which had bugs.

sections.title: What the Survey Tested
sections.content:
The survey ran a simple test suite against each host. For each host, the surveyors tried to open an SMTP connection from ISI-VAXA and separately from ISI-MOE. If either connection succeeded, they then sent three SMTP commands: a VRFY (verify) command for the user postmaster, and an RCPT TO command with a nonexistent mailbox name jqkxwzvb@host to check whether the server would reject unknown users immediately or accept them tentatively.

The test results were recorded with six flags for each host: whether it claimed SMTP support in the NIC host table, whether connections succeeded from each test host, whether VRFY postmaster worked, whether RCPT TO postmaster worked, and whether the server correctly rejected mail to the fake user. This information was gathered from the NIC host table of August 17, 1983, excluding TACs (terminal access controllers) and echo servers.
sections.plainLanguage: They sent each server messages like 'Does postmaster exist?' and 'What about this made-up user?' and wrote down what each server said.

sections.title: Three Significant Problems
sections.content:
The survey identified three classes of bugs that affected about 40 hosts: In reply to RSET (reset) and NOOP (no operation) commands, some servers sent the code 200, which is never legal under RFC 821; they should send 250. VRFY (verify) commands issued before a MAIL command caused some servers to incorrectly reply 554 Nested MAIL command, even though RFC 821 section 4.1.1 explicitly permits VRFY at any point in the session. When a mail transaction had been started with sender and recipient but the message text was not sent before a RSET was issued, some servers sent a delivery failure message to the sender about no message being collected, when RFC 821 specifies that RSET should cleanly terminate the transaction.

Beyond these three major issues, Smallberg noted various other anomalies such as RSET commands causing the connection to close, VRFY POSTMASTER evoking replies with illegal mailboxes, and improper reply codes. Most of these bugs were reported and promptly fixed.
sections.plainLanguage: The main problems were: servers sending wrong answer codes, servers refusing to look up names unless you asked a certain way, and servers complaining about the test command itself.

sections.title: The Numbers
sections.content:
Of 483 hosts tested, 283 were listed in the host table as supporting SMTP, but 49 of those (17%) could not accept a connection from either test host. Conversely, 51 hosts not listed as supporting SMTP did accept connections. A total of 285 hosts could be reached from ISI-VAXA, and 170 of those could also be reached from ISI-MOE; this meant 115 hosts (40%) were reachable only from the Arpanet.

On the 285 connectable hosts: 69 (24%) returned a positive reply to VRFY postmaster, leaving 216 that refused or did not implement VRFY. Of the 285, 162 (57%) immediately rejected mail to the nonexistent user jqkxwzvb, while 115 (40%) accepted such mail. Among the 162 that rejected unknown users, 121 (75%) still accepted mail for postmaster, meaning 42% of all connectable hosts did not immediately reject postmaster.
sections.plainLanguage: Of 483 servers tested, about 1 in 5 that claimed to support email couldn't be reached at all. Of those that worked, only 2 in 5 would reject mail to made-up users, and only 1 in 4 recognized the postmaster account.

references.text: Postel, J., "Simple Mail Transfer Protocol", RFC 821, Network Information Center, SRI International, August 1982.
